claims.text: Controlled slow cooling can convert predominantly straight grain boundaries into serrated grain boundaries in a high-entropy alloy.
Serrated grain boundaries improve toughness retention under elevated-temperature loading.
The proposed benefit of serrated grain boundaries extends to high-strain-rate loading.
The initial Cantor-type CoCrFeMnNi alloy is homogeneous, single-phase, and has predominantly straight grain boundaries.
Slow cooling promotes coarsening of L12-structured gamma-prime precipitates.
Coarse gamma-prime precipitates pin mobile grain boundaries through a Zener-drag-type effect.
Precipitate pinning and differential grain-boundary migration generate a serrated grain-boundary morphology.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute local strain more evenly than straight grain boundaries.
Serration specifically reduces strain concentration at grain-boundary triple junctions.
Reduced strain localization delays intergranular crack nucleation and propagation.
Slow-cooled samples will have higher tensile fracture strain than samples with straight grain boundaries.
Slow-cooled samples will have longer creep rupture life than samples with straight grain boundaries.
Serrated grain boundaries reduce the minimum creep strain rate.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit a more transgranular or mixed fracture mode rather than predominantly intergranular fracture.
The mechanism operates over approximately 600–650 degrees Celsius.
The mechanism should hold broadly for single-phase, multi-principal-element HEAs such as CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed scope assumes that the alloy chemistry permits precipitate formation during slow cooling and that oxidation or other variables do not dominate failure.
The magnitude of improvement and the cooling-rate threshold may vary with composition and processing.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing otherwise identical slow-cooled and moderate-cooled samples while measuring morphology, fracture strain or toughness, creep behavior, and fracture mode.
Failure to produce significantly greater serration or failure to improve the specified mechanical outcomes is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is framed as applying to single-phase HEAs, but its mediator requires formation and coarsening of a distinct gamma-prime precipitate phase. It is not clarified whether 'single-phase' refers only to the initial state or to the alloy throughout treatment and testing.

The conditions emphasize high-strain-rate deformation, whereas creep testing is intrinsically a low-strain-rate/time-dependent test. The experiment does not specify a high strain rate for tensile testing or distinguish the two loading regimes.
